📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

L’Oréal Paris welcomed its latest Women of Worth honorees with an intimate, elegant gala in Los Angeles on Wednesday night. For the annual celebration, which honors unsung nonprofit leaders, guests gathered at The Ebell of Los Angeles, a venue with a rich history of its own.

The evening began with an outdoor cocktail hour, where guests enjoyed passed apps and specialty drinks like the “Parisian Refresher” and “Worth It Spritz” under sparkling bistro lights. As honorees and attendees mixed and mingled, they also had the opportunity to pose for a photographer and peruse a beauty bar stocked with L’Oréal Paris-brand lipsticks, lip oils, and glosses, which were available for guests to take home in a plush velvet bag with “I’m Worth It” embroidered on it.

As the gala officially began inside The Ebell’s picturesque ballroom, longtime brand ambassador Eva Longoria gave the introductory remarks, noting that “this night always gives me goosebumps. I’m always crying.” She saluted her 20-plus-year partnership with the brand and joked that it made her “112 years old,” though she doesn’t look like it, the actor-director said, “because I use Revitalift.” She gave a shout-out to the many beauty influencers in attendance, including Laura Lee and Desi Perkins. “You guys really changed the game of beauty, and I just applaud you,” she said. “Put me in your TikToks.”.

According to recent reports, L’Oréal Paris USA president Laura Branik followed Longoria, emphasizing the brand’s commitment to and pride in its Women of Worth program, which continues to celebrate “the power of women who know their worth and use it,” she mentioned. She then welcomed the company’s newest global ambassador, Kristen Bell, to the stage. Bell, who was attending her “first Women of Worth ever,” said she was “very happy to be here” and introduced moving presentations for the first two honorees: Vy Le of WhereWear, which transforms clothing donations into targeted support for women’s and housing-insecure shelters and the people they serve, and Amanda Rice of The Chick Mission, a nonprofit dedicated to ensuring that every young woman newly diagnosed with cancer has the option to preserve her fertility.

According to recent reports, actor and brand ambassador Aja Naomi King was up next, taking note of the room full of glamorous gowns and festive energy. “Everyone showed up and showed out,” she said, “and we appreciate that because these women deserve to be celebrated properly. I had the immense honor of helping select this year’s Women of Worth, and I keep thinking about how much it matters when someone believes in your potential.” King introduced two honorees: Maya Bird-Murphy of Mobile Makers, an award-winning nonprofit that expands access to design education through workshops, community engagement, public installations, and pop-ups, and Christy Vogel of Sounding Joy, a nonprofit dedicated to providing hearing aids to children whose families cannot afford them.

Longoria then returned to present another pair of honorees: Marisa Hamamoto of Infinite Flow Dance, an award-winning disability-led nonprofit and professional dance company with a mission to reimagine possibilities, one dance at a time, and Chanel Power of Mentor Me Collective, a technical institute transforming how emerging technologists are identified, developed, and positioned to lead.

Sources indicate that during a break in the program, guests enjoyed dinner from a menu that included roast chicken, citrus-soy-and-apple-cider-braised short ribs, and vegan pan-seared “scallops.” Another highlight? The venue’s bathrooms were stocked with more coveted L’Oréal Paris goods like lip oil, mascara, setting spray, and velour puff makeup applicators.

In a recent development, following the break, ambassador, actor, and model Cara Delevingne led the room in a cheerful group proclamation of “We’re worth it!” before introducing her honorees: Emily Cho of Juvie for STEM (JSTEM), an international nonprofit dedicated to expanding access to high-quality STEM education for justice-involved youth, and Arielle Galinsky of The Legacy Project, Inc. (TLP), a national nonprofit connecting younger and older adults for multigenerational friendship and storytelling.

Recent findings suggest that legacy L’Oréal Paris ambassador Andie MacDowell had the pleasure of introducing the event’s final honorees. “For 40 years I have been a part of the L’Oréal Paris family,” she said, with the milestone receiving enthusiastic applause from the audience. “After all these years, the thing that stays with me [about the Women of Worth honorees] is the determination to make life better for someone else. That kind of care is powerful.” MacDowell introduced Jordan Pine of Greenlight Operation, a Pennsylvania nonprofit that strives to strategically combat human trafficking and serve sex trafficked women through a continuum of restorative care, and Dr. Christie Brungardt, cofounder of Jana’s Campaign, a Kansas-based nonprofit dedicated to preventing gender and relationship violence through education.

Proud “newbie” Bell returned to the stage to offer closing remarks and thank all the honorees for their tireless efforts to make life better for others. “I will be thinking of all 10 of these stories and the women we met tonight for quite some time,” she stated. “Even though their stories couldn’t be more different, they seem to have one thing in common: that they all saw what needed to change and they did it. They didn’t wait for someone else to do something; they stepped forward and they did it themselves. And honestly, I think that’s gonna be my biggest takeaway from my first Women of Worth celebration ever: Never underestimate what one woman can set in motion.”.

It has been revealed that each of the 10 Women of Worth 2026 honorees received a $25,000 grant, mentorship, and national visibility. As the program concluded, honorees, their proud guests, and other attendees continued to soak up the special evening and shared in a few more hugs and photo ops. Before departing for the evening, guests were invited to enjoy a final “sweet moment” in a separate room where a colorful candy bar and glasses of Champagne awaited.

Kevin McCallister could be setting another round of traps, as actor Macaulay Culkin is reportedly preparing to return to the Home Alone franchise more than three decades after the original movies — and not just for a McDonald's commercial this time.

According to reports from Puck and Deadline, a upcoming Home Alone sequel is officially in development at Disney, with Culkin returning to his iconic role. Seth Rogen and Evan Goldberg have closed a deal to produce the project through their Point Grey production company and will work with Culkin to develop the screenplay.

Sources indicate that the project builds on an idea Culkin previously pitched to Disney Motion Pictures chief David Greenbaum during a meeting over the summer. The actor, who now has two young sons, has become more receptive to revisiting the franchise and reportedly has a new story in mind.

Rather than another adventure involving a child who is accidentally left home alone, Culkin's proposed concept would follow an older Kevin McCallister as a father. The story would reportedly explore his relationship with his own child, potentially turning the tables on the character who once famously defended his home against burglars.

Culkin last played Kevin in 1992's Home Alone 2: Lost in Upcoming York, which reunited him with director Chris Columbus. The first two films combined to earn approximately $836 million worldwide. There is no word yet on whether Columbus will return for the new installment.

Disney inherited the franchise through its acquisition of 20th Century Fox, but its most recent attempt to revive the series was 2021's Home Sweet Home Alone, which went straight to Disney Plus. Unfortunately, the reboot failed to capture the original's appeal, earning just 15% from critics and 13% from audiences on Rotten Tomatoes.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, the original Home Alone continues to prove its staying power as a holiday favorite. According to FlixPatrol, the 1990 comedy is currently among the most-watched movies on Disney Plus in the United States and internationally.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 has finally arrived, and, to the surprise of no one, it's putting up some big numbers that speak to the pent-up demand. GTA 6 sold more than 30 million copies and hit almost $4 billion on day one, but that's just the start of understanding the impact of the game's release. For starters, the internet service provider Comcast declared that November 18--the final day of preloading--was the busiest day in the manufacturer's history in terms of demand. Peak traffic was 31% higher than an average day and a full 9.6% higher that the previous biggest day ever for traffic to Comcast's network. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Ble-JJxBBGA GTA 6 also now holds five of the top 10 busiest days of Comcast's network of all time. Going further, Comcast stated around 24% of all internet traffic on Comcast's network was people downloading or playing GTA 6 on November 18 (no doubt thanks to the New Zealand trick). Additionally, traffic to Twitch on Comcast's network was up by almost 50% and "is still increasing," Comcast said. A spokesperson for Comcast further contextualized the traffic data, telling GameSpot that between when preloading began on November 10 and through November 18, PlayStation and Xbox traffic pushed enough data on the network for one million homes to stream The Odyssey in 4K repeatedly for two days straight. Comcast was among the internet service providers that offered free speed boosts to subscribers to help them download GTA 6 faster. Additionally, Mat Piscatella of Circana shared data that speaks to the enormity of GTA 6's launch on PlayStation and Xbox. For active accounts November 19 in the US, 61% of PS5 accounts "engaged with" GTA 6. On Xbox, 56% of Xbox players globally did. PS5 players averaged 513 minutes of play for GTA 6 on November 19, compared to 494 on Xbox. These daily active user and minutes played figures are "absolutely bonkers," Piscatella said. GTA 6 was No. 1 on November 19, pushing Fortnite down to No. 2 based on these engagement metrics, Circana said. For more, check out GameSpot’s GTA 6 review and our rundown of the five best things to do first. And if you’re eager for news on GTA 7? Get comfortable, because Rockstar is not going to announce it anytime soon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that google has given its AI-powered "Ask Maps" feature a major upgrade, adding tools for trip planning, real-time route guidance, appointment finding, and saved-list search. The updates begin rolling out today on Android and iOS.

In a recent development, google launched Ask Maps last March as an AI assistant designed to handle questions and requests more complicated than simply searching the word "bar" or "groceries." Instead of performing simple keyword searches, the idea behind Ask Maps is that you can describe several specific requirements at once, and Maps will find places that match them all. For example, you could ask for a restaurant with outdoor seating for a certain number of people, and "Ask Maps" will factor in your past searches and give you results. Of course, AI assistants have a habit of making things up, so even with today's roll-out, you'll want to double-check your sources before you drive an hour to the wrong restaurant.

According to recent reports, to me, this is the most useful upcoming feature launching today. Whether you're planning a day trip for holiday shopping or something more ambitious, like a three-day road trip with coastal hikes and oceanfront dining, Ask Maps will put together a day-by-day schedule. Each plan includes insider tips and numbered map pins for every stop, so you can see the whole route at a glance. Once you're happy with the plan, you can share it with friends and family or export it to Google Docs on desktop.

When it's time to head out, you can ask Maps to pull up your itinerary, or look for the "itinerary" badge in your chat history. You'll see real-time details such as live traffic conditions, whether a place is at the moment open, and even the vibe at your next stop.

Recent findings suggest that intends can change on the fly, too. Ask Maps to add a scenic viewpoint or a lunch spot along the way, then tap to get directions to your next stop straight from the itinerary.

Here's what else you can use Ask Maps to do, starting today.

Industry observers note that pulling up directions now surfaces "Know Before You Go" tips for your route. These include where to park or charge your car, along with real-time conditions like weather, potential delays, and tolls.

Ask Maps is also gaining some agentic capabilities. Allegedly, you can just ask, “Find me a 4 p.m. nail appointment near me,” and Ask Maps will show you open slots across nearby businesses. In addition to finding appointments, Google indicates this agent will be able to call local businesses on your behalf—stay tuned while I wait for the upgrade and test this one out myself.

It has been revealed that if you keep lists of saved places, Ask Maps can now search them for you. Ask something like, "Which spots saved in my lists have availability for 5 in the next 30 minutes?" Ask Maps looks across your lists and checks live availability, so you can pick a place and go.

It has been revealed that these updates start rolling out today on Android and iOS. Travel itineraries and saved-list search are available everywhere Ask Maps is offered. "Know Before You Go" route tips and appointment finding are launching first in the U.S., with more regions coming soon.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Lawrence has helmed almost every film in Lionsgate’s blockbuster series, based on Suzanne Collins’s best-selling novels about a dystopia where a bloodthirsty dictator forces children to fight to the death for the elite’s entertainment.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, when Francis Lawrence, the filmmaker behind The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, greets me over Zoom, he’s aware that his darkly lit, gothic backdrop makes him look a bit like the villainous President Snow. “All I need is a substantial eagle back here,” the white-haired, smartly dressed director jokes.

Lawrence has helmed almost every film in Lionsgate’s blockbuster series, based on Suzanne Collins’s best-selling novels about a dystopia where a bloodthirsty dictator forces children to fight to the death for the elite’s entertainment. He joined the franchise for its 2013 sequel, Catching Fire, and has directed only three non–Hunger Games movies in the decade-plus since. In that time, one could argue, the world has tilted further toward the oppressive future depicted in Collins’s novels—see, for instance, Donald Trump’s Hunger Games–esque Patriot Games. And while Lawrence isn’t naming names, he’s never lost sight of the movies’ larger political message. “I feel really lucky to be able to tell stories that matter, that are wrapped in these commercial packages,” he tells Vanity Fair. “So anytime one of these things comes around, I jump at it.”.

It has been revealed that just as the original Hunger Games film made a star of Oscar winner Jennifer Lawrence (who returns for a scene in the latest movie), Sunrise on the Reaping introduces the world to Australian newcomer Joseph Zada. He plays the younger version of Woody Harrelson’s Haymitch Abernathy, a victor of the Hunger Games who later serves as a mentor to actor Lawrence’s Katniss Everdeen. Making a reflective movie prompted director Lawrence to reflect on his own Hollywood trajectory. “The biggest difference is that I’m a lot more relaxed. I was nervous as hell on Catching Fire,” he notes. “It was my fourth movie. It was a movie I was inheriting. It was a big movie, and it was a massive cast. So I was really intimidated. Now I have much more fun, I will say. I’m much more comfortable with actors, and the amount of actors, and with logistics. And there’s definitely a family that’s built into it, which is very key for me. There’s, what, 14 years of my life spent making these movies? So it has to be fun.”.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: When did you become aware of Sunrise on the Reaping, and at what point did you and Suzanne Collins start discussing an adaptation?

It has been revealed that francis Lawrence: When we did the original series of movies, and we finished the last Mockingjay, she remarked she was done, and we thought that was it. Then she surprised me and Nina [Jacobson], the producer, with Ballad, however many years later. And she never tells us when she’s writing. Even when she has something to read, she never tells us what it’s about. She’s very superstitious about it all. So we got the call, which was very exciting. And she said, “Go to my agent’s house. There’s a manuscript. Let’s talk after you read it.”.

Industry observers note that I got to his house, sat in his backyard, and there was a manuscript and a copy of Catching Fire sitting on top of it with a few tabs in it. I opened to the tabs and saw that it had the portion where Katniss and Peeta were looking up the Haymitch Games, that sequence from the book. And I was like, Oh, she’s written the Haymitch story, which was very exciting. And that started the process that we always have, which is that I read the manuscript in one sitting, then read it a second time after having a conversation with Suzanne.

Then I fly to Fresh York and meet her at Scholastic, and we sit up in a conference room for about a week going through the book, beat by beat, of what we think the movie is going to be. She and I lay it all out and chat, and she sits on her computer and writes a scriptment. Then that’s the thing that we turn over to the screenwriter.

How have you built that trust with the author of these books, having adapted them for more than a decade now?

According to recent reports, that working process happened accidentally when I signed on to do Catching Fire. I had never done a sequel to someone else’s first movie before. And when Lionsgate and the first director, [Gary Ross], parted ways and I got the call, they didn’t have a script, but they had started the process of developing it before I was on board. And so I signed on based on the book and had planned a trip to Upcoming York to meet with Suzanne.

The script came on the day that I was traveling to Latest York. I read it, and it was not the movie that I wanted to make—because I loved the book, and it was not the book. Luckily, nobody else wanted to make that version of the movie either. Our meeting of me just picking her brain turned into, “This script doesn’t work. Let’s go through, page by page, and figure out the version of the movie we want to make.”.

Sources indicate that that’s what really formed the bond—just working really, really closely with her. Spending 8 or 10 hours a day for a week or two in a conference room—me riffing on visual ideas and her talking about the story. We think the same way in terms of storytelling, structure, and she seemed to take to my visual ideas.

Sources indicate that there’s this weird dynamic that happens as we get closer to production. We’re usually developing the script pretty much within a week of shooting. But the production is also building. So you have thousands of people working, figuring out locations, traveling in different parts of the world. The stress levels are building.

Suzanne and I have related the relationship to almost like a mother-son relationship. It starts really lovely and creative, but then as we get closer and closer, it’s me being that late teen who’s ready to leave the home, like, Okay, enough’s enough. I’m going to go make the movie now. I have to say, I love the process. It’s not without its stress sometimes, but that’s part of the closeness of it all that I cherish.

How did this film’s futuristic-meets-1970s aesthetic come about?

Industry observers note that there was an element [of the story] that reminded me a bit of Alice in Wonderland, which then made me think of Jefferson Airplane, that song “White Rabbit,” which brought me to the ’60s and ’70s. Then you can look at characters certain ways. Like, Haymitch, you go, Okay, he’s from, like, young Bruce Springsteen, or Lenore Dove [played by Whitney Peak], like a young Stevie Nicks. And you get this hippie vibe. And the Capitol is that Warhol Studio 54 crowd, and Snow like a ’70s Yves Saint Laurent.

How do you go about casting a young Haymitch, finding an actor who can anchor the film like Jennifer Lawrence did in the original Hunger Games film?

Sources indicate that our casting director, Deb Zane, had met him, and I want to say before he did East of Eden. She had a lot of faith in him. We liked his self-tape a lot. But we knew that he was going to have to pull a lot off. He starts as a very optimistic, fun, playful, young guy in love, and in this movie has to turn into somebody that’s much closer to the Haymitch that we’re used to—cynical and a drunk. He’s going to have to go through a lot of emotional trauma, plus have that kind of mischievousness, irreverence, all these different elements that Woody [Harrelson] has naturally. And so we really put him through the ringer. We did a lot of tests, kept bringing him back, bringing him back, bringing him back. He and I were modulating how much Woody we feel in his performance.

In a recent development, I want to make sure that everybody makes the role their own. That they find the spirit of the character and that it’s not trying to do an imitation of somebody. That’s true of Elle [Fanning] doing Effie, of Ralph [Fiennes] doing Snow, of Jesse [Plemons] doing Plutarch, Kieran [Culkin] as Caesar. Everybody has to figure out how to do it on their own. Then the weird thing is that Kelvin [Harrison Jr., who plays a young Beetee], has worked with Jeffrey [Wright] three times. So he’s fairly close with Jeffrey. When he got the role, he called and noted, “You won’t believe this, but I’m actually playing the young version of you.” He could just conjure Jeffrey Wright. His voice, the speech patterns, the timbre of the sound of everything. It was pretty wild.

Recent findings suggest that were there storylines from the previous films that you felt you could plant Easter eggs for? I’m thinking specifically of the romantic chemistry between Effie and Haymitch.

Recent findings suggest that there are certain Capitol characters where I give a lot of freedom for improvisation. Effie, Caesar, Drusilla [played by Glenn Close], there’s a lot of room for ad-libs. One of the elements that we definitely played with a bit came from an improvised moment in the [last] Mockingjay. We were shooting this scene in Atlanta outside of Snow’s mansion, which is one of the very last scenes of Katniss in the Capitol. She’s saying goodbye to Effie, and then Haymitch and Effie kiss.

Quite honestly, it was an idea because Woody just wanted to kiss Elizabeth Banks. But everybody thought it would be fun and that the fans would dig it, that Haymitch kissed her. Then it became this massive thing of this hidden love that Haymitch and Effie have for one another. And Elle played into that a bit. So there’s, I would say, a hint of flirtation here between the two, less so on Haymitch’s side. His heart is obviously somewhere else in the story. But Elle definitely brought a bit of that to it. That was not scripted. That’s the fun of having great actors.

What was it like to reunite Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, and Woody Harrelson from the original movies?

Jen and I have stayed close over the years. We’ve done four movies together. Josh, who basically has moved to Spain, I haven’t seen in a long time. Woody I see off and on and text every once in a while. But there was something really special about the three of them being back together.

It has been revealed that it’s also really, for the most part, the same crew from 2012, when we started making Catching Fire. It’s the same DP [Jo Willems], the same camera operator [David J. Thompson], the same AD [Christopher Surgent].

According to recent reports, [When] they got to the hotel, Jen and Josh were in the bar having a beer or something, and I was like, Okay, I won’t even shower. I won’t get out of my rain gear. I’ll just come in. The next thing you know, there were 40 of us who had been together since Catching Fire, the gang back together. It’s like a high school reunion or something, but in the best possible way.

There’s a futility to what happens in this film, knowing where we end up in future movies. How do you handle that aspect of history being doomed to repeat itself?

Sources indicate that look, we’re doing a story where you know the lead character is going to make it out. It’s really about how he makes it out, and what he ends up being like at the end of it all. What I’m really pleased about is that the way Suzanne wrote the book, and the way I think we’ve ended the movie, there is a sense of hope that the tragedy is not for nothing. That was really important to me. And one of the beautiful elements in the story, which comes a bit later, is this sense of, everybody has to find their voice. Everybody has to participate.

Recent findings suggest that it really deals with this thing that I think is happening a lot today, where you find apathy: people not wanting to vote, feeling even if they do vote that it’s not going to matter. This idea that you have to be active, and you can’t expect immediate gratification—that everybody needs to stand up and it may take generations, but you still have to do it.

Sources indicate that outside of my screening on the Upper West Side, there was a group protesting Elon Musk and data centers because the documentary about him was playing at the theater. It was a reminder that there will always be something to rise up against, and always people who will be willing to do it.

Industry observers note that yeah, exactly. And ideally, at some point, if everybody stands up, something will change.

According to recent reports, during the 13 years that you’ve worked in this universe, dystopia has felt more and more familiar. How have real-world events influenced your filmmaking?

In the 56 years I’ve been alive, there’s never really been a time where I’ve felt like, Oh wow, everything is great. Nothing is wrong in the world. It always feels like there’s some dystopian sense about the world at any given time. And somehow Suzanne is always able to write these stories about it, which is what makes these movies feel timeless. A lot of people just see them as spectacles, but really they’re about our times very specifically. Almost in a subversive way, I feel like we’ve gotten to smuggle these ideas into these movies that a lot of people go see.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's no secret to anyone who even sort of pays attention to box office happenings that comedy hasn't exactly been booming in recent years. The 2020s have been especially unkind to theatrical comedy, as it's been tough sledding when it comes to comedy for comedy's sake. But "Focker-In-Law" looks to be the rare out-and-out comedy hit when it arrives over Thanksgiving.

It has been revealed that directed by John Hamburg, the fourth entry in the "Meet the Parents" franchise is currently expected to pull in as much as $56 million across the Thanksgiving holiday frame, per Box Office Theory. Mind you, the movie comes out on Wednesday to get in on the holiday, meaning it will have a full five-day Wednesday to Sunday stretch. So, that $56 million figure isn't a standard weekend figure. Meanwhile, the holiday's other big release, the Hailee Steinfeld-led Disney animated flick "Hexed," is targeting a softer opening in the $30 million range.

If all goes well for Universal Pictures, then, "Focker-In-Law" may take the number one spot ... that is, unless Lionsgate has anything to say about it. Indeed, the studio's "Hunger Games" film "Sunrise on the Reaping" is shaping up to be a massive hit, pulling in at least $100 million domestically this upcoming weekend. As such, assuming it's not too front-loaded, it could compete with the Focker family for the crown during its second frame.

According to recent reports, ben Stiller's "Meet the Parents" buried Sylvester Stallone's "Get Carter" at the box office back in 2000, eventually pulling in $330 million worldwide on a $55 million budget. "Meet the Fockers" was an even bigger success, earning over $500 million on an $80 million budget. The problem? By the time "Little Fockers" came along in 2010, the franchise was running out of gas. Against a $100 million budget, it made $310 million.

Industry observers note that to be clear, $310 million is nothing to sneeze at. Nevertheless, "Focker-In-Law," has to pay stars Ben Stiller, Robert De Niro, Blythe Danner, Owen Wilson, Ariana Grande, and (to a lesser degree) Skyler Gisondo, meaning it's likely its budget is once again in the $100 million range.

Recent findings suggest that even so, with an over/under $50 million debut over a typically robust holiday weekend, that's a damn good start. "Moana 2" smashed box office records leading to the biggest Thanksgiving ever in 2024, for example. This year won't be as big, but families go to the movies around the holidays. And when we consider that this franchise has generally performed well overseas, international audiences should turn up as well. (Notably, Paramount is handling overseas distribution.).

Comedy could use a win, too. Earlier this year, two very different comedies in "One Night Only" and "Super Troopers 3" both flopped at the box office on the same weekend. As such, the only true, blue comedy success story of 2026 is "Scary Movie" ($231 million worldwide). Fittingly, that was another revival of an early 2000s-born franchise that's long been dormant. The difference is that we're talking about something more family-friendly with "Fock-In-Law," so that helps.

In a recent development, moreover, most recent comedy hits have been rom-coms like "Ticket to Paradise" ($168 million), "The Lost City" ($192 million), and "Anyone But You" ($220 million). "Focker-In-Law," by comparison, is much more comedy-forward. However, it does have a central romantic element, which should only further aid its cause.

Recent findings suggest that basically, this one has a good shot at attracting audiences eager to catch up with characters they haven't seen in a while, with or without critics on its side. We'll see how everything pans out.

"Focker-In-Law" hits theaters on November 25, 2026.

Kristen Doute can’t help but rock some fabulous fashion after losing 35 pounds.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s no secret that I had a really tough time postpartum after having my beautiful, amazing daughter, Kaia, but I had a really hard time getting rid of the baby weight,” Doute, 43, exclusively shared with Us at her James Mae pop-up shopping event on Thursday, November 19. “I did go on a GLP-1, and I lost a lot of weight. Now I’m really steady and strong, feeling really comfortable with where I’m at. And it does feel good.”.

The Valley star makes it clear that “it’s not about the number on the scale.” Instead, the focus is more on, ‘How do my clothes fit?’”.

“If I’m back in pre-baby sizes, then I’m feeling good about myself,” she remarked from the Y2K millennial bar Zero Lounge in Hollywood.

In September, Doute revealed via Instagram that she had lost more than 30 pounds with help from JoinFridays Telehealth.

While she recommends that every individual consult with their doctor before starting a GLP-1, the former Vanderpump Rules star wants to be open about her experience.

“It was definitely something that worked for me. I tried a lot after having Kaia,” she explained. “The first four or five months, I was eating really well, and I was working out as much as my body would allow me to. And I just saw zero movement in how my clothes were fitting me, and that was something that I decided to do. … It also gave me a lot more energy to want to work out, and it gave me the confidence to want to keep going just from that initial loss of weight.”.

According to recent reports, energy is something Doute needs as she continues to expand James Mae. During her latest shopping event, the designer celebrated the launch of the brand’s Bali Blue colorway and newly introduced parent-and-me shirts.

“The thing that means the most to us is we have a shirt that says ‘I Am Jane Doe,’ and we’ll be gifting all of the profits and all the proceeds to the Time’s Up foundation, which will pay for the legal funds for women [impacted by] sexual assault,” Doute shared. “I [also] really want to make this affordable for everyone. … I don’t think you should have to pay that much for a T-shirt and still get the quality that you love.” (James Mae shirts cost less than $50.).

While Doute is staying mum on how filming a fresh season of The Valley is going — she told Us “there’s a lot more fun this year” — the businesswoman is happy to tease her new “Run It Back” podcast with Katie DiMento.

Premiering Friday, November 20, the project will blend the intersection of sports and pop culture. And yes, Doute will be showcasing her love for the Detroit Lions.

She's rapidly rising in the ranks of TV super-producers, the acerbically funny HBO Max rom-com Youth (in which she also stars) being just the latest.

In a recent development, this earlier series created by and starring Sharon Horgan is a family sitcom that feels far more believable than most, seeing Irish primary school teacher Sharon (Horgan) hooking up with American ad exec Rob (Rob Delaney) over the course of a week, only to discover that she's pregnant once he returns home. They don't really have feelings for each other, but decide to give it a go at being a couple, eventually falling into marriage just before the birth of their child. There are lots of jokes and plenty of acerbic dialogue, but this isn't Married... with Children. Sharon and Rob can be a bit nasty to each other and to their sloppy friend group, but there's also something rather sweet in the show's conviction that having someone to be a mess with can be one of life's great joys. Stream Catastrophe on Prime Video.

Sources indicate that A little more of a high-concept here, but nevertheless an effective show about reimagining yourself in middle age. Younger follows Liza Miller (Sutton Foster), a recently divorced woman in her 40s who finds that age is a barrier to reentering the publishing industry she left years earlier. After a compliment convinces her that she could pass for a younger woman (poor thing), she manages to convince the right people that she's just 26 in order to land an entry-level job. Seven seasons of misadventures ensue, but much of the show revolves around the twisty-turny relationship between Liza and Josh (Nico Tortorella), a tattoo artist in his twenties. Stream Younger on Netflix.

Bridget Everett stars as Sam Miller, who struggles to find her new direction after moving back to her hometown to care for her dying sister. (Don't worry: There's plenty of comedy in the drama, and it's not as heavy as it sounds.) She's solidly middle-aged and starting over, kinda—making new friends in a familiar environment where she has to confront the past and the future alike. Luckily, her love of singing—and a community of goofy oddballs—are there to help. It's another story of a person of a certain age, trying to rebuild their life following an upheaval. Stream Somebody Somewhere on HBO Max.

Recent findings suggest that when all else fails: Start a punk band. This drama from Sally Wainwright (Gentleman Jack) sees five women start a punk band as a lark, just a fun way to kill some time by entering a local talent context. The women realize very quickly, though, that they're very, very pissed off—about the workplace for women, menopause, a diminished dating pool, caring for aging parents and grown children—all of it tied up in the ways in which we treat women, and particularly middle-aged women. The band is a way to reclaim their voices, which doesn't erase or negate any of their problems nor drama (and there's plenty here), but gives them a platform with which to make some noise about it. Stream Riot Women on Britbox.

More of a traditional sitcom, not that there's anything wrong with that, this one builds a lot of goodwill with the performance of Leanne Morgan, its lead and co-creator (alongside Susan McMartin and Chuck Lorre). She plays the show's lead: a Knoxville, Tennessee wife and mom, who finds herself suddenly single in her 50s after her husband of 33 years leaves her. It's a genial, old-school hang-out show with a phenomenal veteran supporting cast that includes Kristen Johnston, Ryan Stiles, and Tim Daly. Stream Leanne on Netflix.

It has been revealed that michele Buteau, who also co-created the series) stars here as a fashion-forward stylist who'd devoted herself to the wrong guy for way too long. As the series opens, Mavis Beaumont is ready for a fresh start, putting herself and her career first—which does not preclude falling into a number of romantic entanglements. As she states more than once, she's going to take on the fashion world with a "body-positive attitude, cute v-neck, and some lip-gloss." Stream Survival of the Thickest on Netflix.

Certainly the goofiest take here on the idea of starting over in mid-life, this is very much a traditional three-camera sitcom, albeit one with a stacked cast of TV legends. Writer Melanie (Valerie Bertinelli), beautician Joy (Jane Leeves), and soap diva Victoria (Wendie Malick) wind up spending a wild night in Cleveland after a plane to Paris is diverted, discovering in the process that, while they're seen as over-the-hill back in Los Angeles, they're all Ohio 10s—though the sassy caretaker of their house, Elka (Betty White), might not agree. Stream Hot in Cleveland on Paramount+.

It has been revealed that she'a s hair younger than Alex, but Fleabag (she's only ever referred to as "Fleabag") is trying to rebuild her life after a bad breakup, with extremely mixed results. This very dark comedy-drama follows a free-spirited, deeply angry single young woman living in London and sharing her romantic ups and downs via confessional asides to us, the audience. She falls, rather reluctantly, for "The Priest" (Andrew Scott)—while she's a confirmed atheist, and he's obviously not, the show doesn't turn aside from the general messiness of the situation. Phoebe Waller-Bridge won separate Emmys as the star, creator, and writer of the series. Stream Fleabag on Prime Video.

Maisel was one of Prime’s first truly buzzy original series, a comedy-drama from Amy Sherman-Palladino (Gilmore Girls) about the title’s Midge Maisel (Rachel Brosnahan), a long-time New York housewife of the late 1950s who discovers a talent for stand-up comedy. Inspired by the real-life careers of comedians like Totie Fields and Joan Rivers, the show is warm and welcoming, with great performances and dialogue; it also achieves something rare in being a show about comedy that’s actually funny. Stream The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel on Prime Video.

The big life change in this earlier Sharon Horgan hit is a little different: Julia Johnstone's mother had been a big help in taking care of Julia's children, but she's not going to do it anymore, leaving this working mom (Anna Maxwell Martin) to take the full brunt of childcare for the first time (her husband in the picture, but not much use). She joins up with other working moms involved with a local support group, including shallow Amanda (Lucy Punch), star of her own ongoing spin-off. Stream Motherland on Prime Video and Britbox.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Happy weekend! Genre fans have plenty to look forward to when it comes to TV. Earlier this week, Netflix revealed the return of 3 Body Project, the heady sci-fi series based on the Liu Cixin novels and adapted by the Game of Thrones showrunners. No big deal. Other series you can look forward to soon include Alien: Earth season 2 and Neuromancer. This month, Blade Runner 2099 is premiering on Prime Video.

And while those releases are still some time away, there’s plenty to tide you over this weekend, including fresh episodes of The Rings of Power, which we’ve discussed over the past week, and new TV highlights premiering or returning. Yellowjackets is back for a fourth and final season. The series picks up as the girls, who’ve been stranded in the wilderness for 19 months, are finally rescued. Meanwhile, in the adult timeline, their lives are falling apart.

In a recent development, percy Jackson and the Olympians is back on Disney Plus. This season follows Percy (Walker Scobell) and Grover (Aryan Simhadri) as they take on their most personal mission yet: rescuing Annabeth (Leah Jeffries) from Kronos.

Other highlights include the fresh Netflix series The Altruists, a biographical drama following the rise and fall of FTX, a cryptocurrency exchange company founded in 2019 that reached a $32 billion valuation. By 2022, the company collapsed after allegations of misusing billions of dollars.

Recent findings suggest that there’s also Dig, the latest TV show from Mike Schur and Amy Poehler. The series marks her first show since Parks and Recreation, and while she’s the lead, she’s also the co-creator and one of the writers. The cast is rounded out by Hugh Laurie and Geraldine Viswanathan, with appearances from Max Greenfield, Jason Mantzoukas, and others.

It has been revealed that we also have a couple of international recommendations: Gordon is an Argentine TV show based on the life and crimes of Anibal Gordon, one of the country's most notorious criminals during the ‘70s and ‘80s. There’s also The Blue Road, a South Korean series set during the 2002 World Cup, where investigators are looking into a string of connected murders in South Korea and Japan. Happy watching.

Yellowjackets is back for one last season. The series, following a team of female soccer players who get stranded in the wilderness after a plane crash, is set across different timelines, following the aftermath of the crash and the lives of the same women 25 years later. The final season finds the survivors finally returning home.

Sources indicate that shauna’s (Melanie Lynskey) life is upended. After reuniting with her ex Melissa (Hilary Swank) and almost killing her, Shauna’s husband Jeff (Warren Kole) and their daughter Callie (Sarah Desjardins) have decided to leave her. She’s going through a midlife crisis, buying a massive pickup truck on the family’s credit card and torturing Jeff in any way she can. Her romantic tensions take up a lot of her narrative, for better or worse. Lynskey is saddled with a lot of Shauna’s shenanigans, which she makes work for the most part. Whether she’s singing karaoke off-tune or stumbling confused into an orgy, Lynskey is hilarious and wounded, and remains a highlight of the series.

It has been revealed that percy Jackson and the Olympians is back with season 3. Based on the beloved Rick Riordan books, the third season adapts the franchise’s third novel, The Titan’s Curse, marking the first time that book has been adapted to the screen.

Based on the real story that was extensively reported on by Upcoming York Magazine, The Altruists follows the relationship between Sam Bankman-Fried (Anthony Boyle) and Caroline Ellison (Julia Garner), two ambitious trading partners who come in and out of their lives while working on FTX, a cryptocurrency exchange company that closed in 2022 after becoming the subject of a cryptocurrency scandal.

Industry observers note that marking Amy Poehler’s comeback to television and her latest collaboration with Mike Schur, Dig follows four women working on an archaeological dig site in Greece. When they find a precious artifact, the women get pulled into an international conspiracy.

Dig doesn't have the deep bench of supporting characters that made Parks and Rec so great, but there are a few decent recurring faces. Kayvan Novak (Nandor in What We Do in the Shadows) is charming as the very Greek mayor of the small town where the show takes place, who has a devastating crush on Elise. Meanwhile, Dropout's Brennan Lee Mulligan has a hilarious guest role as the bumbling fail-son of the rich old man who's been bankrolling the entire dig site. Mulligan's episode in particular, in which the archeologists have to placate an idiotic millionaire in the hopes of getting more funding for their work, feels like a vision of what the show could have been in another timeline where it wasn't bogged down by its serialized drama.

If you’re looking for a foreign crime drama, Gordon is an Argentine crime series following the real-life crimes of Anibal Gordon. The man was one of the most prominent criminals in Argentina during the ‘70s and ‘80s, involved in petty crimes and also in the Dirty War, where members who opposed the government were targeted.

South Korea's latest crime thriller is set against the backdrop of the 2002 FIFA World Cup and follows a string of murders that took place in South Korea and Japan, with the crime scenes having messages written in both languages and uncovering a larger conspiracy.

Industry observers note that ken Burns’ latest documentary explores the criminal justice system in America, diving deep into 250 years of policing, prisons, and more. Apart from being deeply researched, the documentary features voice work from some of the industry’s best actors, including Samuel L. Jackson, Laura Linney, Matthew Rhys, and more.

In a recent development, lastly, if you’re looking for something a little more relaxed, The Circle is back. The reality series, which initially aired on Netflix, has moved to Hulu. After a two-year break, the series is back with the original show’s premise, with contestants participating in a game where they’re all apart, fostering connections through social media, with the ability to catfish others or to play the game as themselves.
